intro: Part II of The Rite of Spring, “The Sacrifice”, opens with a quiet night scene, after which one girl is chosen to dance herself to death. Stravinsky conducts, and the final dance is built from short chords, with plucked cellos and basses playing on the chords.

sections.label: Intro · Night before the sacrifice
sections.mNote: Soft wind chords and divided strings.

sections.label: A · Mystic Circles of the Young Girls
sections.mNote: Six solo violas play the circling tune.

sections.label: B · Glorification of the Chosen One
sections.mNote: Eleven chords introduce the section for the chosen victim.

sections.label: C · Evocation of the Ancestors
sections.mNote: Low brass calls alternate with high woodwind figures.

sections.label: D · Ritual Action of the Ancestors
sections.mNote: Cor anglais melody over horns, pizzicato strings and drums.

sections.label: E · Sacrificial Dance
sections.mNote: Short chords, plucked basses and sudden rests.

cues.title: Introduction to Part II
cues.text: The marking is Largo. Flutes and clarinets play soft repeated chords while the oboes hold long notes, and horns and muted trumpets join them over divided strings. The ballet scenario sets the second part at night.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 86–88, rehearsal figures 79–80, Introduction to Part II: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. The ballet scenario places the second part at night: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The elders in bearskins
cues.text: In Nicholas Roerich’s imagined ancient world, the elders wear bearskins and the girls are gathered into a circle. One girl remains in the middle. The elders watch her final dance.
cues.evidence: Roerich and Stravinsky’s scenario, including the elders in bearskins and the chosen girl’s death, is reproduced in the K catalogue: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring. Van den Toorn, chapter 1, discusses their collaboration and the invented sacrificial rite: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Six solo violas, figure 91
cues.text: At figure 91, Andante con moto, six solo violas play the melody together, each on a different note. Two solo cellos add high harmonics. Stravinsky marks the violas molto cantabile ma non forte.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 96, rehearsal figure 91, Andante con moto; six solo viola parts marked molto cantabile ma non forte, with two solo cellos in harmonics: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sketchbook entry, Clarens, 1912
cues.text: On 17 November 1912, at the Châtelard Hotel in Clarens, Stravinsky wrote in his sketchbook: “with an unbearable toothache I finished the music of the Sacre”.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky’s sketchbook, p. 97, dated 4/17 November 1912; the quoted English translation appears in Van den Toorn, chapter 2, with the Clarens and Châtelard Hotel inscription: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Eleven chords and the Glorification
cues.text: Eleven repeated chords interrupt the circling, with strings, timpani and bass drum striking together. The Vivo follows, a fast dance in bars of changing length, opening with 5/8 and 9/8. The chosen girl stands at the centre while the others acclaim her fate.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 101–02, rehearsal figures 103–104: eleven repeated chords precede the Glorification, which opens with changing 5/8 and 9/8 bars: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. The scenario identifies this dance as the glorification of the selected victim: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Evocation of the Ancestors
cues.text: Bass clarinets and low brass play the invocation, and high winds and brass follow with hard, repeated chords. The phrases are blunt and short.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 115–18, rehearsal figures 121–128, Evocation of the Ancestors: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cor anglais solo
cues.text: Horns, plucked strings and soft percussion play a repeating figure. Above it, the cor anglais plays a short phrase. The accompaniment continues beneath the solo.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 119–21, rehearsal figures 129–131, Ritual Action of the Ancestors; the cor anglais enters over repeated horn, pizzicato-string and percussion figures: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Concert performance, Paris, 1914
cues.text: On 5 April 1914 Pierre Monteux conducted The Rite of Spring in concert at the Casino de Paris. Afterwards admirers carried Stravinsky on their shoulders, less than a year after the uproar at the ballet’s première.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 1, p. 6, recounts the 5 April 1914 concert under Monteux and Stravinsky’s being carried on the shoulders of admirers: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Opening of the Sacrificial Dance
cues.text: The last dance begins with short, sharp chords. Cellos and basses play pizzicato beneath them. Rests separate the chords, and the next one enters before a regular pattern can form.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, pp. 39–41, describes the opening of the 1943 Sacrificial Dance and its pizzicato cellos and basses, rehearsal figures 1–9 in that edition: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html. The K catalogue identifies the revised finale in this January 1960 performance: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Revision of the final dance, 1943
cues.text: In 1943 Stravinsky revised the bars, note values and scoring of the final dance. Much of the notation was doubled in size, so that quavers became crotchets. This 1960 performance uses that revision.
cues.evidence: Van den Toorn, chapter 2, pp. 39–54, documents the 1943 revision, including the doubled note values: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html. The K catalogue specifies this text for the recording made on 5–6 January 1960: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring

transitions.title: Six solo violas at Andante con moto
transitions.to: A · Mystic Circles of the Young Girls
transitions.how: The low horn phrases of the introduction die away. At Andante con moto, six solo violas begin a harmonised melody, with high cello harmonics around it and low strings beneath. The violas are marked molto cantabile ma non forte.

transitions.title: Eleven chords into the Glorification
transitions.from: A · Mystic Circles of the Young Girls
transitions.to: B · Glorification of the Chosen One
transitions.how: Climbing runs lead into eleven hammering chords in strings, timpani and bass drum. The other winds and brass are silent for these chords. The Glorification then begins at Vivo, with short orchestral bursts and changing bar lengths.

transitions.title: General pause before the summons
transitions.from: B · Glorification of the Chosen One
transitions.how: A general pause separates the Glorification from the summons, between rehearsal figures 120 and 121. Bass clarinets and low brass enter over held low strings, followed by higher wind and brass chords. The new crotchet equals the preceding dotted quaver, so the pulse carries across the silence, and the phrases become broader.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 114–15, rehearsal figures 120–121, including the general pause and dotted-quaver-to-crotchet tempo equation: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf

transitions.title: Invocation to Ritual Action at Lento
transitions.to: D · Ritual Action of the Ancestors
transitions.how: The invocation slows to Lento, with descending figures in the bassoons. The Ritual Action opens with an accompaniment of low horns, plucked strings and percussion. A cor anglais melody enters above it.

transitions.title: Into the final dance
transitions.from: D · Ritual Action of the Ancestors
transitions.how: Winding phrases for clarinet and bass clarinet fade over the low, quiet accompaniment of the ritual. The final dance cuts in with short orchestral chords, sharpened by pizzicato cellos and basses. The bar lengths change and abrupt rests break up the chords. The girl’s solo begins over this irregular metre.
transitions.evidence: The closing Ritual Action is shown in the full score, p. 128, rehearsal figures 140–141: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. For the different 1943 finale used here, Van den Toorn, pp. 39–41, documents the opening chords and pizzicato low strings: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html. Recording version: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: Composer of dance music in which a single displaced accent could unsettle the dancers, and of a psalm setting that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
Stravinsky was born in 1882 at Oranienbaum. His father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre in St Petersburg; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. He entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks are short orchestral works. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. A full ballet, The Firebird, followed. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he recalled that the rehearsals ended with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
